Mockup for sign-off · 3 September 2026 · drawn from the running platform

The plan table's squeeze

With the pen open, the columns that hold words give up their width to the columns that hold controls. Below about 1,300 px a tactic's title wraps one character per line. Every figure and every picture below comes from the real page with clean values — no line breaks anywhere.

“are you sure of your fix? this is a zoomed page”

01What is actually happening

The control columns hold about 600 px of near-fixed width — Target 224, Owner 155, Collabs. 92, Quarters 132 — in a table that has only 762–1,085 px to spend. The prose columns absorb the entire shortfall, and the growing box (which is sized to what is in it) then reports a height for a column two characters wide.

Page widthTactic columnTallest row
1400269191
1300192313
12001151957

Zooming reduces the effective page width, which is why this appears when you zoom and not at 100 % on a wide window. Reading mode is not affected — with the pen shut the Tactic column is still 273 px at 1,200.

02Three ways the width can come back

All three put a floor under the two prose columns (200 px for the tactic, 140 for the outcome) so they stop absorbing the shortfall. They differ in where the width comes from, and that is the decision.

A · The target boxes narrow

The four boxes in the Target cell drop from 96 px to 76. Nothing moves, nothing folds — the cell simply asks for less.

Page widthTactic column Tallest rowTable
1400296171fits
1300216251fits
1200200313runs 43px past the pane

Cost It buys the least: 27 px at 1,400 and 85 at 1,200, and at 1,200 the table still runs 43 px past its pane, which is the one thing the plan tables may not do.

B · The target block stacks Fits at every width

The Target cell becomes one column of four boxes instead of two by two. It gives back 101 px and costs height in that cell only.

Page widthTactic column Tallest rowTable
1400345163fits
1300265211fits
1200200313fits

Cost Rows get taller where the target cell is now the tallest thing in the row — at 1,400 every row settles at 163 px whether or not its title is long.

03The other lever: height

Your point stands and it is a different axis. The description sits inside the tactic cell, so it never buys width — hiding it takes the column from 115 px to 107 at 1200 and to nothing at all at 1100. What it buys is height, and that is worth having on its own terms: more rows on the screen at once.

So it should be capped rather than hidden. The description shows one line until the cursor is in it, then it opens to its full size. Nothing is hidden, nothing becomes unreachable, and the row stops paying for prose nobody is reading right now.

At 1200 wideTactic columnTallest row Three rowsTable
Today1151957— fits
Height only — description capped200191 491runs 83px past the pane
C — the tail folds283242 668fits
C + capped description283201 565fits

At 1300 the same pair reads 364 px / 170 for C alone and 364 px / 149 with the description capped — three rows in 428 px instead of 491.

The height lever cannot stand alone. With the prose floor in place and nothing given back by the controls, the table runs 83 px past its pane at 1200 — the one thing these tables may not do. It is a companion to a width fix, not a substitute for one.

04Sequence: which rung comes first

You suggested the target block first and the tail after it. Measured across six widths and two content shapes, it goes the other way — and the reason is height, not width.

Page widthTodayB · target stacks C · tail foldsB + C
1920 · short titles547 / 92 589 / 163711 / 129 766 / 163
1400269 / 191345 / 163 431 / 170485 / 170
1300192 / 313265 / 211 364 / 171431 / 170
1200115 / 1957200 / 313 283 / 210365 / 171
1100over 9pxover 82px 203 / 311284 / 210

Tactic column width / tallest row, both in px. Long titles except where noted.

B is the expensive rung, not the gentle one

Four stacked boxes are a floor: B reports h=163 at every width, both content shapes. On a wide window with short titles today's row is 92 px — B makes it 163 whether or not anything is wrong, and C makes it 129. And B alone cannot reach the narrow end: it runs 82 px past the pane at 1100, where C still fits.

Which is why the ladder is C first

C buys more width per unit of height, and it is the one that survives the narrow end. B then earns its place below 1200, where C alone leaves a 311 px row and the pair brings it to 210.

" alt="B and C together at 1100">

And nothing changes on a full-size window

At 1920 today's row is the shortest of all four. Every treatment costs height, so applying either one above the threshold would make a big screen worse to fix a problem it does not have. The rungs are gated on width, and a wide window keeps exactly the table it has today.

05What I would do, and why

A ladder in three steps, gated on width. Above 1400 nothing changes at all. Below 1400 the tail folds under the name (C) — 431 px of title at 1400, 283 at 1200. Below 1200 the target block also stacks (B) — 365 px at 1200 and 284 at 1100, with rows at 171–210 against today's 1,957. The capped description rides on whichever rung is active and gives back most of what the strip costs in height. B is the honest fallback for the middle widths, where the tail still fits and only the target block needs to give way. A is the weakest: it buys 27 px and still runs past the pane at 1,200.

Both keep every control reachable, which is the rule that governs this table — the four target boxes are the only way to set a target, so they may narrow or stack but never disappear while the pen is open.

Two things to decide before I build:

  1. Where the tail goes at the narrow end. In C the collaborators picker and the four quarter marks sit under the name, as a strip. They lose their column headings there, so they would need naming in place — a short label before each, or a line of their own.
  2. Where the switch happens. At 1,300 the table is still comfortable in B and generous in C. I would fold the tail only below 1,280 and narrow the target block between 1,280 and 1,400, so a full-size window never changes shape.
